rationale: A wins because it treats the missing accuracy data as the story constraint, not a decoration. Its best line, "It won't say how often it's wrong," is the hard journalist question; B's "concrete evidence the category is moving from drafting tasks into liability-bearing decisions" takes one product launch and inflates it into a trend piece. B has usable bones, but A is the one a founder could act on without walking into unsupported claims.
gaps_in_A: "automating that call across 150 jurisdictions" overstates the update slightly; Deel is said to flag risks and check classification, not make the legal classification decision.

"One employer, one bad contractor call" is a smart ladder-down angle, but it is not alive until a named customer and real flag exist. A says that, but keeping it as a top angle still risks false confidence.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the second angle. This is pricing and bundling strategy, not funding mechanics.
The legal angle needs one more proof demand: who maintains changing labor-law and tax content across 150 countries after launch.
gaps_in_B: "AI wants to automate" is cute copy, not a sober angle. Worse, "deciding whether your contractor is legally an employee" overstates a risk-flagging tool into a decision-maker.

"concrete evidence the category is moving from drafting tasks into liability-bearing decisions" invents a broader market shift from one Deel launch. That is how trend pieces get laughed out of inboxes.
"betting the feature is worth more as lock-in than as revenue" assigns strategy Deel did not state. Ask the question; don't print the answer in the headline.
"tracks all 150 in real time" is not in the update. The facts say the tool checks exposure across 150 countries as a company hires; real-time legal maintenance is a proof question, not a fact.
